Human beings therefore have no eternally unchanging essence. They can change even in their essential qualities.
We will see in the Phenomenology how negativity operates. For now, I will give only two examples.

From the beginning of its historical existence, humanity has been divided into two “classes”: slaves and masters. An individual had necessarily to be either master or slave, insofar as we consider him as a historical human being, just as he had necessarily to be either female or male insofar as we consider his animal reality.

In one form or another, this division into classes persisted throughout the centuries of human history. We can therefore say without exaggeration that “mastery” and “slavery” became essential qualities of human existence.
And yet there now exists in the USSR a socialist society that had never existed before, a society containing neither masters nor slaves but free and equal citizens.

This therefore provides factual proof—against bourgeois thinkers who denied the dialectical character of human beings—that the supposedly “eternally unchanging” human “nature” or “essence” can itself change without human beings ceasing to be human.
It changed under the influence of revolutionary struggle, which, as we will see, is the first and primary manifestation of negativity.

We saw that the nature or “essence” of a non-dialectical thing is determined by its “place” in the cosmos. Human beings, as animals, also possess such a nature. The human being is a “land-dwelling animal.” The human body is shaped by this fact and, like the body of every land animal, is poorly adapted to living underwater or in the air.
That is how the human body was, is, and will remain.

And yet, insofar as human beings inhabit a technical world—that is, insofar as they are human beings in the proper sense—they occupy the air, notably by means of airplanes, and live underwater, for example in submarines.
They achieve this through technical work, which, as we will see, is a fundamental but secondary manifestation of negativity.
Human beings do not grow wings or fins. Their bodies remain what they are. And yet human beings cease to be merely “land animals” and become, in addition, animals of “water” and “air.”

The existence of a dialectical being is therefore not finally and irrevocably determined by the “natural” or “essential” place it occupies in the world. It can change the human “nature” determined by that place and, so to speak, cross the boundaries prescribed for it by the world.

This means that a dialectical or “negative” being changes not only in the way a non-dialectical thing changes—that is, as a result of interactions imposed on it from outside, through the effects of all the other things in the cosmos. It also changes from within itself, without any external necessity, or, as philosophy puts it, “spontaneously” or “freely.”
We can therefore say that a dialectical being has no “nature” given to it once and for all by who knows whom—God—or by who knows what—the “cosmos,” “nature,” and so on.
Instead, we must say that it creates or produces itself, along with its own “essential” qualities, and that it changes itself in an essential way.
This self-creation and this creative—that is, essential—self-transformation are themselves manifestations or acts of negativity.
More precisely, insofar as negativity is not nothing but something, it is nothing other than this essential self-creation, this transformation of dialectical being.
So, to define negativity, we can use Hegel’s somewhat paradoxical formula and say that negativity is the capacity of a dialectical being “not to be what it is and to be what it is not.”
This capacity also distinguishes a dialectical being from a non-dialectical thing, which always remains equal to itself and can therefore be only what it is.
Since, as we will see, negating desire is the first and simplest manifestation of negativity, we can modify Hegel’s definition and remove some of its paradoxical form.
We can say that negativity gives a dialectical being the ability not to want to be what it is, and to want to be what it is not.
And it is easy to see that this desire to negate one’s own “essence” or “nature” is characteristic of human beings, and of human beings alone.
There is an old Jewish joke.
A son is reading a book and asks his father:
“A woodpecker?” the father replies. “Oh, a woodpecker iz a fisch.”
“What are you talking about? It says here that it sits in a tree!”
“Well,” says the father, “es iz a meshugener fisch”—it’s a fish that has lost its mind.

Strictly speaking, if we saw a fish so much as trying—or wanting—to live the life of a bird, we would have to say either that it had lost its mind or that it was really a human being that happened to look like a fish.
But madness is an illness, and nature removes sick individuals from its environment by killing them. So there will be no fish that flies and no bird that lives underwater.
If a human being actually becomes amphibious, then, this means that this animal has “lost its mind” and yet has still managed to survive within the natural world.

The titanic power—work and struggle—that allowed human beings to impose their “madness” on the natural world, and not only to survive in that world despite this madness but to alter the world in accordance with it, is precisely what Hegel calls negativity.
This human negativity is expressed with unusual precision and radical force by one of the characters in Kurt Weill and Bertolt Brecht’s opera Mahagonny.
Someone tries to shake him morally by saying, as people often do, “Be a man!”
“But I don’t want to be a man at all” (Ich will ja gar kein Mensch sein).

And we know that such a radically “negating” desire is not always an unrealizable Nietzschean dream of “superhumanity.” It can also take the form of a kind of negative realization in Kirillov-like suicide: suicide without a cause, in the natural sense of the word.

In any case, dialectic—dialectical existence or dialectical being—is produced by the dominance of negativity over identity. In other words, it depends on a being’s ability to create itself, or to change “spontaneously”—that is, “freely,” independently of “physical” causes—its own essential qualities and characteristics: precisely those features that, in a non-dialectical thing, would be called its “nature” or “essence.”
But I repeat: this dominance of negativity over identity necessarily presupposes that identity itself is also present in dialectic—in dialectical existence and in the dialectical being.
In other words, a dialectical being necessarily contains at least two fundamental categories.
But if both are present, there must also be a third and final fundamental dialectical category: the category that unites them, which Hegel calls totality (Totalität).
Identity forces a thing to remain the same. Negativity allows it to change essentially.
Because a dialectical being contains both identity and negativity, it must therefore remain the same despite its essential changes, and it must change essentially despite remaining the same.

The difference between a Greek slave and a free citizen of the socialist state may be far more “essential” than, say, the difference between a snail and a chimpanzee. Yet the slave and the citizen are both human beings.
And even if, by some unimaginable and impossible “miracle,” a snail became a chimpanzee, it would thereby cease, finally and irreversibly, to be a snail.
This kind of identity is therefore fundamentally different. It is called totality.

“Inessential” changes—that is, non-dialectical or natural changes—are called inessential precisely because they are compatible with the given “essence” or nature of a thing. Their occurrence therefore leaves that essence untouched and unchanged.

Dialectical changes, by contrast, are negative—“negating”—precisely because they negate the essence itself and are incompatible with it. When they occur, the essence changes. And because an essence is, by definition, what does not change, the being from which this process begins ceases, at the very moment negativity is realized, to be what it was.
It disappears, and another being appears in its place as its “negation.”
If this being nevertheless remains in some sense “the same,” its unity must therefore contain two essentially different beings. It is the unity of a certain multiplicity: a “whole” composed of parts.
It is, in other words, a totality.
We can say that dialectical being differs from non-dialectical being because it is always total: it always contains three fundamental categories.
If it contained only identity, it would be a non-dialectical or natural being and would never change essentially.

If it contained only negativity, it would not exist at all. If there is nothing, there is nothing to negate, and the result of such a negation is nothing. Or, by negating nothing—which is precisely not negating—it is, so to speak, equal to zero.
So in order to be dialectical—in order to be something rather than nothing—a dialectical being must contain both identity and negativity.

But an identity that has been changed “essentially,” that is, changed through negation, is no longer the eternally unchanging identity of a non-dialectical thing. It is no longer the identity that existed, so to speak, before the appearance and realization of negation.
We now have a different category: a new, third category, totality.

Like identity, totality makes a being equal to itself, makes it remain what it is. But this equality is actually the result of an equation between two essentially different beings: the first dominated, so to speak, by identity, and the second by negativity.

And because the result of this equation is dominated by neither of the first two categories, we can say that equating these two opposed beings produces a new being, a third being, in which totality dominates.

But in reality only this “third” being genuinely exists, and only it is dialectical. Only it realizes the dialectic. Without it, the first being would simply be non-dialectical, while the “second” would not exist at all.
We must therefore say that real dialectical being is always total.
Within a total being, however, one of its three aspects can predominate.
If its identity with itself predominates, it is called a thesis.
If its negativity predominates—that is, its creative self-negation—it is called an antithesis.
And if its totality predominates—that is, if it preserves itself within its own negation and preserves that self-negation within itself—it is called a synthesis.
The “first” thesis and the “first” antithesis are, strictly speaking, abstractions. They do not really exist.
Dialectical being is, as it were, “produced” at the moment when thesis and antithesis unite in synthesis.

And this synthesis, because it really exists—that is, because it belongs to the identical natural world—is fully equal to itself. Identity therefore predominates within it, which makes it a really existing thesis.
This real thesis can then really negate itself. Negativity now predominates within it, so it becomes a really existing antithesis.
But because it is already “total”—because it still contains identity—it really unites within itself both itself, as a real antithesis, and the real thesis it negates.
It therefore becomes a second really existing synthesis.
The same thing can then happen to this synthesis as happened to the first, and so on.
This sequence of real theses, antitheses, and syntheses—that is, the totality in its thētic, antithetic, and synthetic forms—is also called the real dialectic.
But we can also say that each individual totality is itself a realization of dialectic.
And conversely, every total being is necessarily dialectical: it realizes the dialectic because totality necessarily includes the other two fundamental dialectical categories as well.
We can therefore say that a dialectical being is dialectical because it is total.
But totality would not be totality if it did not include negativity.
If negativity were removed, there would be no difference between synthesis and thesis—that is, between totality and the original identity.

Identity would remain eternally unchanged. It would no longer be the first fundamental dialectical category but simply non-dialectical identity, eternally equal to itself, uniting no multiplicity and therefore incapable of forming a “totality.”
This is why I said from the beginning that the source, the nerve, or the driving force of dialectic is negativity.
But if negativity in a sense produces dialectical being—or, if you prefer, transforms a non-dialectical, “identical” thing into a dialectical being—then that being really exists only as a totality.
We can therefore say that real dialectical being is nothing other than existing totality.
This means, first, that unlike a non-dialectical thing, dialectical being contains not one but three fundamental categories.

Second, its existence is always the result of some movement, process, or becoming (Werden) that necessarily includes an element of self-negation, whereas a non-dialectical thing remains equal to itself “for ever and ever,” unchanged.

The Marxist proletarian, for example, negates himself as a proletarian by becoming a socialist—that is, classless—citizen. More exactly, he becomes one through the active negation of his own proletarian condition.
Finally, dialectical being is, so to speak, circular.
By negating its own self-affirmation, it affirms itself again and therefore affirms itself. It returns, so to speak, to its point of origin.

A non-dialectical thing, by contrast, never negates itself and therefore never “leaves” itself. And because it never leaves itself, it cannot return to itself either. Its existence is like a “point,” not a circle.
I have said that only the human being is such a dialectical—that is, total—being. More precisely, humanity as a whole is the real dialectic.
